## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The documentation presents Behaviour-Driven Development as "the software development process that Cucumber was built to support", adding "There's much more to BDD than just using Cucumber." [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Behaviour-Driven Development"). BDD "closes the gap between business people and technical people" [V] through collaboration across roles to build shared understanding, rapid small iterations, and system documentation automatically checked against the system's behaviour; the means is concrete, real-world examples of how the system should behave, used to guide work from concept to implementation [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "What is BDD?"). It enhances an existing agile process rather than replacing it, as "a set of plugins for your existing process" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "BDD and agile").

Day-to-day work runs as three practices in order: Discovery (talk about concrete examples of a small change), Formulation (document them in a form that can be automated) and Automation (implement each example starting from an automated test) [AR] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices"). The documentation holds that the order matters: formulating before effective discovery is "a waste of time", and automating after the code is written is test automation, "but it's not BDD" [V] (docs/bdd/myths.md). Gherkin, "a medium that can be read by both humans and computers" [V], carries the formulation; its writing guidance says to describe behaviour rather than implementation, keep examples concrete and free of technology assumptions, phrase the same thing the same way, and check outcomes on observable output, with implementation details kept in step definitions [AR]. The source is product documentation with no studies or measurements: its recommendations are practitioner assertions, not demonstrated findings.

## The three practices

Discovery comes first. Documentation and automated tests are "nice side-effects" [V]; the real goal is valuable working software, reached fastest through conversations between the people who imagine and deliver it [AR] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Discovery: What it _could_ do"). Structured discovery workshops, focused on real-world examples from the users' perspective, grow shared understanding of users' needs, the rules the system follows and the scope of the work; they may "reveal gaps in our understanding, where we need more information before we know what to do" [V], and often surface low-priority functionality that can be deferred out of a story [AP]. Newcomers should start here: "You won't get much joy from the other two practices until you've mastered discovery." [V]

Formulation turns each valuable example into structured documentation that confirms the team shares an understanding, in a medium the whole team can read and that can later be automated; writing it together builds a shared language that "helps us to use problem-domain terminology all the way down into the code" [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Formulation: What it _should_ do"). Automation takes one example at a time, connects it to the system as a test that fails because the behaviour does not exist yet, then develops the code, guided as needed by lower-level examples of internal components [AP] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Automation: What it _actually does_"). "The automated examples work like guide-rails, helping us to keep our development work on track." [V] Later they help the team understand what the system does and change it safely, and their "rapid, repeatable feedback reduces the burden of manual regression testing" [V]. Over time the documented examples become an asset: "The code reflects the documentation, and the documentation reflects the team's shared understanding of the problem domain." [V] (docs/bdd/index.md, "Three practices").

## Collaboration: who does what

The Three Amigos is "a meeting that takes user stories and turns them into clean, thorough Gherkin scenarios" [V] with "three voices (at least)" [V]: the product owner decides scope; the tester generates scenarios and edge cases, asking how the application will break; the developer adds steps and thinks through how it will execute [AP]. Because each sees the product differently, it is essential that all these roles discover examples together [AR], and the meetings need not be limited to three people or held only once (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "The Three Amigos"). The whole team should write Gherkin together at first; later a developer and a tester can pair on it, provided the product owner actively reviews their output [AP] (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing Gherkin").

A discovery workshop is "a conversation where technical and business people collaborate to explore, discover and agree as much as they can about the desired behaviour" [V] for a story. It is held "As late as possible before development on a new User Story begins" [V], with "3-6 people" [V] including the Three Amigos, for "about 25-30 minutes per story" [V]; needing longer suggests the story is too large or missing specifics and should be split or set aside for research [AP] (docs/bdd/discovery-workshop.md). Without it, the conclusion warns, teams "won't discover any unknowns" [V]. Example Mapping makes the acceptance-criteria conversation "short and very productive" [V]: the story on a yellow card, each rule (acceptance criterion) on a blue card, examples on green cards under their rule, and questions that cannot be answered in the session on red cards, continuing until the scope is clear or time runs out [AP] (docs/bdd/example-mapping.md, "How it works"). OOPSI Mapping and Feature Mapping are named as other workshop models [BT].

## Writing scenarios

"Your scenarios should describe the intended behaviour of the system, not the implementation." [V] `When "Bob" logs in` is a functional requirement; a five-step walk through a login form is a procedural reference, and "procedures belong in the implementation details" [V]. The test for any clause: "Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?" [V] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Describe behaviour"). A declarative style is less brittle and reads better as living documentation; imperative tests "communicate details, and in some contexts this style of test is appropriate" [V] but are tied to the current UI and "often require more work to maintain" [V]. In the declarative subscription example, exact values and the mechanics of logging in live in the step definitions, so "The intent of the scenario remains the same, even if the implementation changes later." [V] (docs/bdd/better-gherkin.md, "Consider a more declarative style").

Good examples are concrete (names, places, exact dates and amounts) and "don't mention technical details" [V]; the admonition "Imagine it's 1922" asks for examples that assume no technology (docs/bdd/examples.md). A feature's `In order to`, `As a` and `I want` lines "cover Why, Who, and What" [V], and the scenarios supply the How. A scenario that cannot be described in one sentence is "probably trying to cover too much" [V]; a step containing "and" should usually be split; and "Cucumber features are best served by consistency" [V], so one phrasing per meaning (docs/bdd/who-does-what.md, "Writing features"; "Scenarios").

## Myths

Four myths are named (docs/bdd/myths.md): that the practices can be taken in any order, answered with Liz Keogh's line that "having conversations is more important than capturing conversations is more important than automating conversations" [V] [BT]; that automating scenarios after the code is BDD ("a perfectly reasonable way to do test automation, but it's not BDD" [V]); that discovery needs no conversation, since teams that leave examples and scenarios to one person are "not BDD" [V] and discovery must bring together "representatives of the different specialists who all need to share understanding about what will be built" [V]; and that using Cucumber means doing BDD, which the page denies [AP].

## History

BDD was pioneered by Daniel Terhorst-North in the early 2000s, as a response to test-driven development, and "has evolved into both analysis and automated testing at the acceptance level" [V] [BT]. JBehave (2003) replaced "test" with "behaviour" vocabulary; the Given/When/Then template "was developed to capture a story's acceptance criteria in an executable form" [V], influenced by ubiquitous language from Eric Evans' *Domain-Driven Design* and by the Connextra user-story template credited to Rachel Davies [BT]. RSpec followed in 2005; Cucumber began as Aslak Hellesøy's better Story Runner, since "the RSpec Story Runner was for the whole team, including non-coding stakeholders" [V] (docs/bdd/history.md).

## Gherkin: structure and keywords

Gherkin's keywords give structure to executable specifications; most lines start with one, comments start a line with `#`, and two-space indentation is recommended [AP]. Each step's text after its keyword is matched to a step definition, and a colon after a keyword that should not have one means "your test(s) will be ignored" [V] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Reference"). Primary keywords: `Feature` (first in the file, one per file, with an optional free-form description that Cucumber ignores at runtime but reports show); `Rule` (from Gherkin 6, one business rule and the examples that illustrate it); `Example`/`Scenario`; the steps `Given`, `When`, `Then`, `And`, `But` and `*`; `Background`; `Scenario Outline`/`Scenario Template`; and `Examples`. Secondary: Doc Strings, Data Tables, tags and comments [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Keywords"; "Feature"; "Rule").

An example is specification, documentation and test at once, and "we recommend 3-5 steps per example" [V], since too many steps lose its expressive power [AP]. `Given` puts the system into a known state without user interaction; `When` is an event, from a person or another system; `Then` uses an assertion to compare actual with expected outcome, on observable output (a report, user interface or message) [AP] "and not a behaviour deeply buried inside the system (like a record in a database)" [V]; on checking the database, "resist that temptation!" [V] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Example"; "Given"; "When"; "Then"). Keywords are ignored when matching, so the same text under `Given` and `Then` is a duplicate, which the page argues forces a clearer domain language [AR] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Steps"). `Background` holds the `Given` steps every scenario shares, which the page reads as "incidental details" [V]; it should be short (consider moving details if it runs past 4 lines), vivid and only as complicated as the client needs to know [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Background"; "Tips for using Background"). A `Scenario Outline` runs once per row of its `Examples` table, its `<>` parameters replaced before matching [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Scenario Outline"; "Examples").

## Step arguments, languages and step organization

Doc Strings (between triple quotes or backticks, with significant inner indentation) and Data Tables (with escapes for newline, pipe and backslash) pass larger data to a step definition as its last argument [AP] (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Step Arguments"). Gherkin should be written in the language users and domain experts use about the domain, which is why it has been translated into "over 70 languages" [V]; a `# language:` header sets it, defaulting to English (docs/gherkin/reference.md, "Spoken Languages"; docs/gherkin/languages.mdx, "Localisation").

Step definitions should be grouped by domain concept, one file per major domain object as a rule of thumb, which avoids the "Feature-coupled step definitions" anti-pattern [AP] (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Grouping step definitions"). "Don't write step definitions for steps that are not present in one of your scenarios." [V] Similar steps can be collapsed into one parameterised step backed by helper methods; "Your step definitions are the glue to the actual code" [V], hiding implementation details, and Cucumber "is a DSL wrapper around the programming language whose full expressiveness remains available to you in the step definition files" [V], not in feature files (docs/gherkin/step-organization.mdx, "Writing step definitions"; "Avoid duplication"; "Helper methods").

## Key Connections

- Fred Brooks, *The mythical man-month*: the epigraph to Discovery, on deciding precisely what to build [BT].
- Liz Keogh: quoted to answer the first myth; named as a BDD pioneer and early JBehave contributor [BT].
- Daniel Terhorst-North and "Introducing BDD" (2006): credited with pioneering BDD and starting JBehave [BT].
- Test-driven development: BDD grew as a response to it [AP].
- Eric Evans, *Domain-Driven Design* (ubiquitous language) and Rachel Davies' Connextra user-story template: credited as influences on Given/When/Then [BT].
- RSpec and its Story Runner: what Cucumber set out to improve on [AP].
- Example Mapping, Event Storming, OOPSI Mapping and Feature Mapping: named as techniques for discovering examples [AP] [BT].
- An article at geepawhill.org: linked for lower-level examples of internal components [BT].

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. The practices are ordered: discovery before formulation before automation; formulating without discovery is "a waste of time" [V].
2. Automating scenarios after the code is written is reasonable test automation, but not BDD.
3. Discovery left to one person is not BDD; it must be a conversation across specialists.
4. Using Cucumber is no proof of doing BDD.
5. Scenarios describe behaviour, not procedures; imperative UI steps are brittle, though they suit some contexts.
6. `Then` steps check observable output, not the database.
7. Step definitions are grouped by domain concept, not by feature.
